subject: history
title: Cambridge IGCSE History (0470)

officialDocument.title: Cambridge IGCSE History 0470 syllabus for 2027 and 2028 (version 1, published September 2024)
officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Option, key question and depth study headings are transcribed from the subject content of the official syllabus with their printed letters and numbers (Option A key questions 1-6, Option B key questions 1-6, Depth studies A-E with key questions 1-4 and 3(a)/3(b) for Germany). The syllabus prints no content codes: node codes (A1, B4, DS-B3a) and objective codes (A1.1 = Option A, key question 1, first focus point) are ours. Objectives paraphrase the printed focus points and node descriptions summarise the specified content in our own words; the 'Historical skills' node is ours (from assessment objective AO3). No syllabus text is reproduced.
notes: Read 2026-10-08 from the official PDF (version 1, published September 2024, for exams in 2027 and 2028; June and November series, and March in India): content overview, assessment overview and objectives, the whole subject content, details of the assessment (including the prescribed topics for Paper 2) and the changes page ('no significant changes which affect teaching').

This version is examined from 2027. A candidate sitting the examination in 2026 is examined on the previous syllabus (for 2024-2026), which is not in the repository; the syllabus states there are no significant changes affecting teaching, so the content here also serves 2026 candidates, but the prescribed Paper 2 topics differ by year.

Optional structure: all candidates study EITHER Option A (the nineteenth century, 1848-1914) OR Option B (the twentieth century, international relations since 1919) of the Core content (option group 'core-content'), AND at least one of the five Depth studies A-E (option group 'depth-studies'). Coursework candidates may instead base Component 3 on a centre-devised depth study, which is not modelled.

Assessment overview as read: all candidates take Paper 1 Structured Questions (2 hours, 60 marks, 40%: Section A has eight questions, four on Option A and four on Option B, two from key questions 1-3 and two from 4-6 in each option, answer any two; Section B has two questions on each depth study, answer one; every question is a structured essay in three parts (a), (b) and (c); AO1 and AO2) and Paper 2 Document Questions (1 hour 45 minutes, 40 marks, 30%: one question on the prescribed topic of Option A or of Option B, each with up to seven sources and five parts; AO1 and AO3), and EITHER Component 3 Coursework (40 marks, 30%: one piece of extended writing of up to 2,000 words on the significance of an individual, group, development or event, from a depth study; internally assessed, externally moderated) OR Paper 4 Alternative to Coursework (1 hour, 40 marks, 30%: two questions on each depth study, answer one; parts (a), an account (AO1), and (b), the importance of a person, organisation, development or event (AO2)). Grades A* to G. AO weightings: AO1 30%, AO2 45%, AO3 25% overall (Paper 1: 33/67/0; Paper 2: 20/0/80; Component 3 and Paper 4: 38/62/0).

The marks of the parts are not printed in the syllabus. Our practice items assume Paper 1 (a) 4, (b) 6, (c) 10 (20 per question); Paper 2 five parts of 7, 8, 7, 8 and 10 marks; Paper 4 (a) 16 and (b) 24. A reviewer must check these against current specimen papers and mark schemes.

Prescribed topics for Paper 2 as printed: 2027 Option A: How was Germany unified? (March, India), the overseas empires key question (June), the 1848 revolutions (November); Option B: Versailles (March, India), the USSR's control over Eastern Europe (June), Versailles (November). 2028 Option A: Italy (March, India and June), the causes of the First World War (November); Option B: the Cold War (March, India and November), Hitler's foreign policy (June).
Command words printed: describe, discuss, explain; phrases such as 'How far do you agree...?' and 'Write an account...' may also be used.

Shared with the ZIMSEC syllabus: the causes of the First World War (Option A key question 6), the Versailles settlement, the League, Hitler's foreign policy and the origins of the Cold War (Option B key questions 1-4), the Cuban Missile Crisis (key question 5), the rise and rule of the Nazis (Depth study B key questions 2 and 3(a)) and Russia (Depth study C). Concepts taught only for ZIMSEC (Zimbabwean, African and other world history) are not tagged to this syllabus. Component 3 Coursework is not simulated.
overview: Cambridge IGCSE History studies world history in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Candidates take one Core content option: Option A, the development of modern nation states 1848-1914 (the 1848 revolutions, the unification of Italy and of Germany, the American Civil War, nineteenth-century imperialism and the causes of the First World War), or Option B, international relations since 1919 (the Treaty of Versailles, the League of Nations, the road to war in 1939, the origins of the Cold War, American containment in Korea, Cuba and Vietnam, and Soviet control of Eastern Europe). They also study at least one depth study: the First World War, Germany 1918-45, Russia 1905-41, the United States 1919-41, or the Second World War in Europe and the Asia-Pacific.
assessmentOverview: All candidates take Paper 1 Structured Questions (2 hours, 60 marks, 40%: two core-content questions and one depth-study question, each in three parts) and Paper 2 Document Questions (1 hour 45 minutes, 40 marks, 30%: one question with up to seven sources on the prescribed topic of the candidate's option). They also take either Component 3 Coursework (an essay of up to 2,000 words, 40 marks, 30%) or Paper 4 Alternative to Coursework (1 hour, 40 marks, 30%: one two-part question on a depth study).

components.name: Paper 1: Structured Questions
components.description: Section A: eight questions on the Core content (four on Option A, four on Option B), answer two. Section B: two questions on each of the five depth studies, answer one. Each question is a structured essay in parts (a), (b) and (c).

components.name: Paper 2: Document Questions
components.description: One question on the prescribed topic of Option A or of Option B (the topic changes each series), with up to seven sources and five parts.

components.name: Component 3: Coursework
components.description: One piece of extended writing of up to 2,000 words on the significance of an individual, group, organisation, development, place or event, from a syllabus or centre-devised depth study. Taken instead of Paper 4. Internally assessed, externally moderated.

components.name: Paper 4: Alternative to Coursework
components.description: Two questions on each of the five depth studies; candidates answer one. Each question has part (a), an account, and part (b), on the importance of a person, organisation, development or event. Taken instead of Component 3.

topics.name: Core content Option A: The nineteenth century: the development of modern nation states, 1848-1914
topics.description: Candidates study EITHER Option A OR Option B of the Core content (Paper 1 Section A and Paper 2).

children.name: Were the revolutions of 1848 important?
children.description: Specified content: the nature of the 1848 revolutions and the influence of liberalism and nationalism; causes, events and results in France, Italy, Germany and the Austrian Empire; reasons for failure. (Italy and Germany in 1848 are taught with key questions 2 and 3.)

objectives.text: Explain why liberalism and nationalism had grown in influence by 1848.
Explain why so many revolutions broke out in 1848 and what they had in common.
Explain why most of the revolutions failed.
Assess what, if anything, the revolutions changed.

children.name: How was Italy unified?
children.description: Specified content: Austrian influence over Italy; Italian nationalism and Mazzini; events of 1848-49; Victor Emmanuel II and Cavour, Plombières and the war with Austria in 1859; Garibaldi and the invasion of Sicily and Naples; the Kingdom of Italy and the completion of unification by 1870.

objectives.text: Explain why Italy was not unified in 1848-49.
Assess how important Garibaldi's contribution was to unification.
Assess whether Cavour helped or hindered unification.
Explain how important moves towards Italian unification were for other European countries.

children.name: How was Germany unified?
children.description: Specified content: German nationalism; the Zollverein; the 1848 revolution in Prussia; the Frankfurt Parliament and its failure; Austrian influence restored by 1850; Bismarck as Minister-President and his foreign policy to 1871 (Schleswig-Holstein, the Austro-Prussian War, relations with France, the Spanish succession and the Franco-Prussian War, the German Empire).

objectives.text: Explain why Germany was not unified in 1848-50.
Explain how Bismarck brought about Austria's defeat in 1866.
Explain how Bismarck brought about France's defeat in 1870.
Assess how far Bismarck was responsible for German unification.

children.name: Why was there a civil war in the United States and what were its results?
children.description: Specified content: causes and consequences of the American Civil War, 1820-77: differences between North and South; slavery, slave and free states, abolitionism; the 1860 election and secession; reasons for the North's victory; the role of Lincoln; Reconstruction and its success.

objectives.text: Assess how far slavery caused the Civil War.
Explain the significance of Lincoln's election as president.
Explain why the North won the war.
Assess whether the war changed anything.

children.name: Why, and with what effects, did nations gain and expand their overseas empires in the nineteenth century?
children.description: Specified content: economic, military, geopolitical, religious and cultural motives; French assimilation and direct rule (Faidherbe and Senegal), British indirect rule (Lugard and Nigeria) and Belgian private imperialism (Leopold II and the Congo) and their impacts on Africans; the British in India and 1857; the wars of independence in the Philippines and Cuba, the Spanish-American War and the Treaty of Paris, the US debate on imperialism, the Philippines under American control, American intervention in Cuba to 1906.

objectives.text: Explain the motives behind European and US imperialism.
Assess how varied the impacts of European imperialism on Africans were.
Explain why Indians resisted British rule and with what effects.
Explain why, and with what effects, the United States gained former Spanish colonies.

children.name: What caused the First World War?
children.description: Specified content: the origins of the war, 1890-1914: the alliance system and European diplomacy; the 1902 Anglo-Japanese Alliance; the arms race; colonial rivalries; developments in the Balkans; the crisis of June-July 1914 and the outbreak of war.

objectives.text: Assess whether the alliance system and global diplomacy made war more or less likely.
Assess how far colonial problems created tension between the Great Powers.
Explain why problems in the Balkans were so hard for the Great Powers to solve.
Explain how the assassination of Franz Ferdinand led to war.

topics.name: Core content Option B: The twentieth century: international relations since 1919
topics.description: Candidates study EITHER Option A OR Option B of the Core content (Paper 1 Section A and Paper 2).

children.name: Was the Treaty of Versailles fair?
children.description: Specified content: the roles of Wilson, Clemenceau and Lloyd George; the terms of the Treaty; its social, economic and political impact in Germany to the end of 1923; contemporary opinions about the Treaty.

objectives.text: Describe the motives and aims of the Big Three at Versailles.
Explain why the victors did not get everything they wanted.
Explain the impact of the Treaty on Germany up to the end of 1923.
Assess whether the Treaty could be justified at the time.

children.name: To what extent was the League of Nations a success?
children.description: Specified content: the League's structure, aims and membership; peacekeeping in the 1920s (Vilna 1920, the Aaland Islands 1920-21, Corfu 1923, Bulgaria 1925); humanitarian work (refugees, health, working conditions, slavery); the 1930s: causes, events and consequences of the Manchurian and Abyssinian crises.

objectives.text: Assess how far weaknesses in the League's organisation and membership made failure inevitable.
Assess how successful the League's peacekeeping was in the 1920s.
Assess how important the League's humanitarian work was.
Explain how far the Depression made the League's work more difficult in the 1930s.

children.name: How far was Hitler's foreign policy to blame for the outbreak of war in Europe in 1939?
children.description: Specified content: Hitler's foreign policy aims; rearmament; the Saar; the remilitarisation of the Rhineland; the Rome-Berlin Axis and the Anti-Comintern Pact; German and Italian involvement in the Spanish Civil War; the Anschluss; the Czechoslovakian crisis and the Munich Agreement; the Polish crisis and the outbreak of war.

objectives.text: Explain the long-term consequences of the Treaty of Versailles.
Explain the consequences of the League's failures in the 1930s.
Assess whether appeasement was justified.
Assess how important the Nazi-Soviet Pact was.
Explain why Britain and France declared war on Germany in September 1939.

children.name: Who was to blame for the Cold War?
children.description: Specified content: the origins of the Cold War: the 1945 summit conferences and the breakdown of the US-Soviet alliance in 1945-46; Soviet expansion into Eastern Europe to 1948 and American reactions; the occupation of Germany and the Berlin Blockade; NATO and the Warsaw Pact.

objectives.text: Explain why the US-Soviet alliance began to break down in 1945.
Explain how the USSR had gained control of Eastern Europe by 1948.
Explain how the United States reacted to Soviet expansion.
Explain the consequences of the Berlin Blockade.
Assess whether the United States or the USSR was more to blame for starting the Cold War.

children.name: How effectively did the United States contain the spread of communism?
children.description: Specified content: case studies: American reactions to North Korea's invasion of South Korea, UN involvement and the course of the war to 1953; American reactions to the Cuban Revolution, including the Missile Crisis and its aftermath; American involvement in Vietnam, including reasons, tactics and strategy, and reasons for withdrawal.

objectives.text: Assess how effectively the United States contained communism in Korea, 1950-53.
Assess how effectively the United States dealt with Cuba, 1959-62.
Explain American involvement in Vietnam, 1955-75, and why the United States withdrew.

children.name: How secure was the USSR's control over Eastern Europe, 1948-c.1989?
children.description: Specified content: resistance to Soviet power in Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968); the Berlin Wall; Solidarity in Poland; Gorbachev and the collapse of Soviet control over Eastern Europe.

objectives.text: Explain why there was opposition to Soviet control in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968, and how the USSR reacted.
Compare events in Hungary in 1956 and in Czechoslovakia in 1968.
Explain why the Berlin Wall was built in 1961.
Explain the significance of Solidarity in Poland for the decline of Soviet influence.
Assess how far Gorbachev was personally responsible for the collapse of Soviet control over Eastern Europe.

topics.name: Depth study A: The First World War, 1914-18
topics.description: Candidates study at least one depth study (Paper 1 Section B; Component 3 or Paper 4).

children.name: Why was there stalemate on the Western Front?
children.description: Specified content: the Schlieffen Plan in practice (Belgium, the BEF, Russian mobilisation); Mons, the Marne, the race to the sea and the First Battle of Ypres; trenches and attrition; trench warfare; tanks, machine guns, aircraft and gas; Verdun and the Somme and Haig's leadership.

objectives.text: Explain why the Schlieffen Plan failed.
Explain why a defensive war had emerged by the end of 1914.
Describe what living and fighting in the trenches was like.
Assess how important new methods of warfare were.
Explain the significance of the battles of Verdun and the Somme.

children.name: To what extent was it a world war?
children.description: Specified content: British Empire troops on the Western Front (Indian and Canadian case studies); the war in Africa (German East Africa, South West Africa); Japan in Asia (Tsingtao, sea lanes); the Arab Revolt.

objectives.text: Assess the importance of British Empire troops on the Western Front.
Describe the contribution of Indian and South African troops in Africa.
Assess Japan's contribution to the Allied victory.
Assess how important the Arab Revolt was.

children.name: How important were other fronts?
children.description: Specified content: the war at sea (Jutland, convoys, submarines and the U-boat campaign); the Gallipoli campaign; the Eastern Front and the defeat of Russia; the impact of war on civilians.

objectives.text: Assess who won the war at sea.
Explain why the Gallipoli campaign of 1915 failed.
Assess how important the Eastern Front was.
Explain the impact of the war on civilian populations.

children.name: Why did Germany ask for an armistice in 1918?
children.description: Specified content: the German offensive of 1918 and the Allied advance; the impact of American entry; conditions in Germany (the Kiel mutiny, the German revolution, the Kaiser's abdication); the Armistice.

objectives.text: Explain the importance of America's entry into the war.
Explain why the German offensive of 1918 failed.
Explain why revolution broke out in Germany in October 1918.
Explain why the Armistice was signed.

topics.name: Depth study B: Germany, 1918-45
topics.description: Candidates study at least one depth study (Paper 1 Section B; Component 3 or Paper 4).

children.name: Was the Weimar Republic doomed from the start?
children.description: Specified content: the 1918 revolution and the Republic; the Versailles settlement and German reactions; the Weimar Constitution, political divisions and the army; political disorder 1919-23 (left and right, economic crisis and hyperinflation, the Ruhr); the Stresemann era (economic and foreign policy achievements); cultural achievements.

objectives.text: Explain how Germany emerged from defeat at the end of the First World War.
Explain the impact of the Treaty of Versailles on the Republic.
Assess how far the Republic recovered after 1923.
Describe the achievements of the Weimar period.

children.name: Why was Hitler able to dominate Germany by 1934?
children.description: Specified content: the early Nazi Party (ideas and methods, the Munich Putsch, the roles of Hitler and other leaders); the impact of the Depression (the crisis of 1930-33, reasons for the Nazi rise, Hitler takes power, the Reichstag Fire and the 1933 election). The consolidation of 1933-34 is taught with key question 3(a).

objectives.text: Describe what the Nazi Party stood for in the 1920s.
Explain why the Nazis had little success before 1930.
Explain why Hitler was able to become Chancellor by 1933.
Explain how Hitler consolidated his power in 1933-34.

children.name: The Nazi regime: (a) How effectively did the Nazis control Germany, 1933-45?
children.description: Specified content: Nazi rule (the Enabling Act, the Night of the Long Knives, the death of Hindenburg, the removal of opposition, methods of control and repression, culture and the mass media); anti-Semitism and the persecution of minorities; opposition to Nazi rule; the Final Solution.

objectives.text: Assess how much opposition there was to the Nazi regime.
Explain how effectively the Nazis dealt with their political opponents.
Explain how the Nazis used culture and the mass media to control the people.
Explain why the Nazis persecuted many groups in German society.
Assess whether Nazi Germany was a totalitarian state.

children.name: The Nazi regime: (b) What was it like to live in Nazi Germany?
children.description: Specified content: economic policy including rearmament; the experiences of women and young people; the impact of the Second World War on Germany (the war economy).

objectives.text: Explain how young people reacted to the Nazi regime.
Assess how successful Nazi policies towards women and the family were.
Assess whether most people in Germany benefited from Nazi rule.
Explain how the coming of war changed life in Nazi Germany.

topics.name: Depth study C: Russia, 1905-41
topics.description: Candidates study at least one depth study (Paper 1 Section B; Component 3 or Paper 4).

children.name: Why did the Tsarist regime collapse in 1917?
children.description: Specified content: the main features of Tsarist rule and Russian society before 1914 (the 1905 Revolution and its aftermath, attempts at reform); the First World War and its impact on the Russian people; the March Revolution of 1917 (taught with key question 2).

objectives.text: Assess how well the Tsarist regime dealt with the difficulties of ruling Russia up to 1914.
Explain how the Tsar survived the 1905 Revolution.
Assess how far the Tsar was weakened by the First World War.
Explain why the March 1917 revolution succeeded.

children.name: How did the Bolsheviks gain power, and how did they consolidate their rule?
children.description: Specified content: the Provisional Government and the Soviets; reasons for its failure; the Bolshevik seizure of power and the role of Lenin; Bolshevik rule, the Civil War and War Communism; the Kronstadt Rising and the New Economic Policy.

objectives.text: Assess how effectively the Provisional Government ruled Russia in 1917.
Explain why the Bolsheviks were able to seize power in November 1917.
Explain why the Bolsheviks won the Civil War.
Assess how far the New Economic Policy was a success.

children.name: How did Stalin gain and hold on to power?
children.description: Specified content: Lenin's death and the struggle for power; reasons for Stalin's emergence by 1928; Stalin's dictatorship (terror, the Purges, propaganda and official culture).

objectives.text: Explain why Stalin, and not Trotsky, emerged as Lenin's successor.
Explain why Stalin launched the Purges.
Describe the methods Stalin used to control the Soviet Union.
Assess how complete Stalin's control was by 1941.

children.name: What was the impact of Stalin's economic policies?
children.description: Specified content: the modernisation of Soviet industry; the Five-Year Plans; collectivisation; life in the Soviet Union (social groups, ethnic minorities and women).

objectives.text: Explain why Stalin introduced the Five-Year Plans and collectivisation.
Assess how successful Stalin's economic changes were.
Explain how the Soviet people were affected by these changes.

topics.name: Depth study D: The United States, 1919-41
topics.description: Candidates study at least one depth study (Paper 1 Section B; Component 3 or Paper 4).

children.name: How far did the US economy boom in the 1920s?
children.description: Specified content: the expansion of the economy (government policies, mass production of cars and consumer goods, older industries, credit and hire purchase, the decline of agriculture); weaknesses in the economy by the late 1920s.

objectives.text: Explain the factors on which the boom was based.
Explain why some industries prospered while others did not.
Explain why agriculture did not share in the prosperity.
Assess whether all Americans benefited from the boom.

children.name: How far did US society change in the 1920s?
children.description: Specified content: the 'Roaring Twenties'; film and other media; Prohibition and gangsterism; immigration restrictions, the Red Scare and religious intolerance; discrimination against Black Americans; the Ku Klux Klan; the changing roles of women.

objectives.text: Describe the 'Roaring Twenties'.
Assess how widespread intolerance was in US society.
Explain why Prohibition was introduced and later repealed.
Assess how far the roles of women changed during the 1920s.

children.name: What were the causes and consequences of the Wall Street Crash?
children.description: Specified content: the Wall Street Crash and its financial, economic and social effects; Hoover's reaction; the 1932 presidential election and the two candidates' programmes.

objectives.text: Assess how far speculation was responsible for the Crash.
Explain the impact of the Crash on the economy.
Explain the social consequences of the Crash.
Explain why Roosevelt won the 1932 election.

children.name: How successful was the New Deal?
children.description: Specified content: Roosevelt's inauguration and the 'Hundred Days'; New Deal legislation, the 'alphabet agencies' and the changes they caused; opposition (Republicans, the rich, business, the Supreme Court, radical critics such as Huey Long); strengths and weaknesses in dealing with unemployment and the Depression.

objectives.text: Describe the New Deal as introduced in 1933.
Explain how far the character of the New Deal changed after 1933.
Explain why the New Deal met opposition.
Explain why unemployment persisted despite the New Deal.
Assess whether the New Deal was a failure because it did not solve unemployment.

topics.name: Depth study E: The Second World War in Europe and the Asia-Pacific, 1939-c.1945
topics.description: Candidates study at least one depth study (Paper 1 Section B; Component 3 or Paper 4).

children.name: How did the Second World War in Europe develop?
children.description: Specified content: the extent of German conquest in 1940 (the fall of France and Vichy, Dunkirk, Operation Sea Lion, the Battle of Britain); Operation Barbarossa and initial Nazi successes; defeat at Stalingrad and its impact.

objectives.text: Assess to what extent Nazi Germany had gained control of Europe in 1940.
Explain why Germany was unable to conquer Britain.
Explain why Hitler invaded the Soviet Union in 1941.
Explain why the Battle of Stalingrad was a turning point.

children.name: How did the Second World War in the Asia-Pacific develop?
children.description: Specified content: reasons for and consequences of the attack on Pearl Harbor; reasons for initial Japanese successes in Southeast Asia by early 1942 (case study: Malaya and Singapore); the Battle of Midway and its impact.

objectives.text: Explain how US-Japanese relations deteriorated.
Assess how successful the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor was.
Explain why the Japanese were successful in the early stages of the war.
Explain why the Battle of Midway was a turning point.

children.name: What was the impact of war on civilian populations in Europe and the Asia-Pacific?
children.description: Specified content: the impact of bombing (the Blitz, Allied bombing of German cities); Japanese control (case study: Malaya and Singapore); Nazi control in occupied Europe (case study: Poland, including the circumstances leading to the Holocaust and its impact); resistance movements in Malaya and France.

objectives.text: Explain the impact on civilians of the bombing of Britain (1940-41) and Germany (1943-45).
Explain how Japanese control affected people's lives.
Describe the experiences of civilians in Nazi-occupied Europe.
Assess how effective resistance movements were in Europe and the Asia-Pacific.

children.name: How did the Allies achieve victory over the Axis powers?
children.description: Specified content: the invasion of Sicily and victory in Italy; the collapse and surrender of Germany in 1945 (D-Day and the advance to Germany, the Russian advance); the defeat of Japan (Guadalcanal and Okinawa, island-hopping, bombing, the atomic bomb); consolidation of victory (occupations of Germany and Japan, the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials).

objectives.text: Explain the importance of the Allied advance through Italy.
Explain why Nazi Germany was on the point of collapse by April 1945.
Explain why the Allies achieved victory over Japan.
Explain how the Allies consolidated their victories in Germany and Japan.

topics.name: Historical skills: using sources as evidence
topics.description: Not a content section of the syllabus: this node is ours, from assessment objective AO3 (understand, interpret, evaluate and use a range of sources as evidence in their historical context), which Paper 2 tests. The source skills it covers apply to whichever core option the candidate studies.

objectives.text: Understand and interpret sources, making inferences about their message and purpose.
Evaluate the reliability and usefulness of sources in their historical context, and compare sources.
Use a range of sources, with contextual knowledge, to reach a supported judgement.
